title: A literal quote mark inside a CSV field is written as two quote marks, not a backslash-escaped one
assumption: A quote character inside a CSV field is escaped the way it is in most languages, with a backslash.

input.description: A CSV export of a field whose text contains a literal double-quote character, e.g. a product name like `Say "hello"` or a quoted phrase inside a review.

what_goes_wrong: A field containing a literal `"` is represented in CSV as `""` (two quote characters) inside the surrounding quoted field, not `\"` - code that naively strips a single leading/trailing quote and un-escapes backslash-quote sequences (a common pattern borrowed from JSON/string literals) will mangle the field instead of recovering `Say "hello"`.
why: RFC 4180's escape mechanism for a literal double-quote inside a quoted field is to double it - `""` means one literal `"` - with no backslash involved anywhere in the format. A real CSV parser (Python's `csv` module) recognizes a `""` sequence while inside a quoted field as an escaped quote and collapses it to one `"` in the field's value; it is a dialect-specific rule that has nothing to do with how any programming language escapes string literals.
fix: Use a real CSV parser that implements RFC 4180's doubled-quote escaping, rather than any backslash-based unescaping borrowed from another format. If writing CSV by hand, double every `"` inside a field and wrap the whole field in quotes.

sources.title: RFC 4180: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files
Python docs: csv - CSV File Reading and Writing

test_cases.note: A CSV-parsing function given this text must collapse the doubled quotes into one literal quote character inside the field value.
